faq.a: Ferritin reflects stored iron; low levels are highly specific for deficiency unless inflammation is present.
faq.q: Why is ferritin the best screening test?

faq.a: Absorption is best on an empty stomach; if GI upset occurs, give with a small amount of fruit juice for vitamin C.
faq.q: Can oral iron be given with food?

faq.a: When oral iron is ineffective, poorly tolerated, or rapid repletion is needed (e.g., pre‑operative anemia).

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with fatigue and pallor; ferritin is 12 µg/L. What is the next step? — Identify and treat the underlying cause of iron loss before starting supplementation.

A patient with severe IDA has a normal ferritin due to recent malaria infection. How do you interpret the result? — Recognize inflammation can mask low ferritin; use transferrin saturation and clinical context.
Why is ferrous sulfate preferred over ferrous gluconate in most low‑resource settings? — Higher elemental iron content reduces pill burden and cost.
A child with hookworm infection and IDA is started on oral iron but shows no rise in Hb after 2 weeks. What should you do? — Switch to IV iron or treat heavy hookworm load aggressively.
How does iron deficiency contribute to cardiac complications? — Chronic hypoxia leads to high-output cardiac failure and tachycardia.
Differentiate IDA from anemia of chronic disease using lab values. — Low ferritin in IDA vs normal/high ferritin in ACD; transferrin saturation is low in both but CRP is elevated in ACD.
What red‑flag symptom in a patient with IDA mandates urgent referral? — New chest pain or syncope suggesting myocardial ischemia.
Explain why vitamin C improves oral iron absorption. — It reduces ferric to ferrous iron, enhancing duodenal uptake.
ai.title: Iron Deficiency Anemia
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is the most common nutritional anemia worldwide, especially in low‑resource settings. It results from inadequate iron stores leading to microcytic, hypochromic red cells and impaired oxygen delivery.

b: Hemoglobin <13 g/dL (men) or <12 g/dL (women)
Serum ferritin <30 µg/L (or <15 µg/L in infection‑free settings)
Low transferrin saturation (<15 %)
sections.p: IDA is a decrease in hemoglobin due to depleted iron stores. Diagnosis requires low hemoglobin plus laboratory evidence of iron deficiency.

b: Mild: Hb 11–12 g/dL (women) or 12–13 g/dL (men)
Moderate: Hb 8–10 g/dL
Severe: Hb <8 g/dL with symptoms
sections.p: Severity is graded by hemoglobin level and clinical impact.

b: Inadequate dietary iron (plant‑based diets low in heme iron)
Helicobacter pylori or hookworm infection causing chronic GI loss
Menstrual loss or postpartum hemorrhage
Malaria‑related hemolysis with iron loss
Chronic kidney disease (reduced erythropoietin)
sections.p: In East Africa the leading causes are dietary deficiency, chronic blood loss, and infections.

b: Pale conjunctivae and nail beds
Koilonychia (spoon nails) in chronic cases
Glossitis and angular cheilitis
sections.p: Patients develop fatigue, pallor, dyspnea on exertion, and in severe cases, tachycardia and cardiac murmurs.
Targeted tests confirm iron deficiency and rule out other microcytic anemias.

t.b: Is anemia present and what is the red cell morphology? → Microcytic, hypochromic RBCs suggest IDA or thalassemia.
Are iron stores depleted? → Low ferritin confirms deficiency; if infection present, interpret with caution.
Is iron transport impaired? → <15 % supports IDA.
Is there chronic GI loss? → Positive test prompts endoscopic evaluation.
Is parasitic blood loss present? → Positive exam directs anti‑helminth therapy.

b: Chest pain or syncope (possible myocardial ischemia)
Rapidly falling hemoglobin despite oral therapy
Signs of heart failure (edema, jugular venous distension)
sections.p: Severe IDA can precipitate cardiac failure and increase peri‑operative risk.

b: Intravenous iron sucrose or ferric carboxymaltose if malabsorption, severe anemia, or oral intolerance
Address chronic bleeding: deworming, H. pylori eradication, surgical control of bleeding lesions
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, replace iron, and monitor response.

b: Repeat CBC and ferritin at 4–6 weeks
Encourage consumption of meat, legumes, vitamin C‑rich fruits to enhance absorption
Annual deworming in endemic areas
sections.p: Re‑check hemoglobin and ferritin after 4 weeks of therapy; educate on iron‑rich foods and deworming.

b: Thalassemia trait – normal ferritin, family history, target cells on smear
Anemia of chronic disease – ferritin normal/high, low transferrin saturation, inflammatory markers elevated
sections.p: Other microcytic anemias share similar labs but differ in cause.

b: Acute infection can falsely elevate ferritin; consider CRP or repeat after infection resolves
Peripheral smear may show normocytic cells early in deficiency

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain or severe dyspnea
Signs of heart failure (edema, rapid breathing)
